# unreal-agent-tui

A terminal UI for the [unreal-agent](https://github.com/unreallabsai/unreal-agent)
harness — a pair-programming agent for your project, in the style of a coding CLI.

Two binaries:

- `unreal-tui-agent` — headless runner: the harness plus added **Read**, **Write**,
  and **Edit** file tools on top of the built-in Bash/ViewImage tools. Accepts a
  JSON request, streams session items as JSONL, and persists resumable sessions
  under `<workspace>/.harness/sessions`.
- `unreal-tui` — the bubbletea terminal UI. Spawns `unreal-tui-agent` per turn
  and renders the transcript, tool calls, and responses.

## Build

Requires Go 1.27+.

```sh
go build -o bin/ ./cmd/...
```

## Run

```sh
export OPENAI_API_KEY=...            # or OPENROUTER_API_KEY / FIREWORKS_AI_API_KEY
zua -workspace ./my-project
zua -workspace ./my-project -provider openrouter -model google/gemini-2.5-pro
```

Keys: `Enter` sends, `Esc` aborts the running turn (or quits when idle), `Ctrl+C` quits.

The headless runner also works standalone:

```sh
zua-agent -workspace ./my-project -p 'Summarize this project.'
```

## Architecture

```
cmd/unreal-tui          bubbletea UI (internal/tui)
cmd/unreal-tui-agent    headless harness runner (internal/runner)
internal/filetools      Read/Write/Edit tool translators + operation manager wrapper
```

The runner wires the public unreal-agent packages directly (coordinator, inbox,
contextbuilder, session store, LLM clients) and wraps the local operation
manager so file operations execute durably like shell operations. Sessions
resume by `session_id`, which the TUI tracks across turns.

Providers: `openai` (default), `commandcode`, `openrouter`, `fireworks`, `ollama` — set via
request field or `UNREAL_TUI_PROVIDER`; model via `UNREAL_TUI_MODEL` or request.

## UI features

- Markdown rendering (glamour) with syntax-highlighted code blocks
- Tool-call cards: Bash commands, Read/Write paths, and colorized `- / +` diffs for Edit
- Session usage in the status line (tokens in/out for the last turn)
- Slash commands: `/new`, `/resume` (session picker), `/model [id]`, `/help`, `/quit`
- Growing multiline editor (Enter sends; Alt/Shift+Enter for newline)
- Tool calls and statuses appear as they happen; see DESIGN.md for the
  streaming notes (token-level streaming is deferred to upstream harness support)

## Cost: pristine vs file tools

The harness's published cost savings assume a minimal tool surface. By default
this project runs the **pristine** configuration (Bash + ViewImage + skills,
upstream system prompt) — matching the benchmarked setup. Opt into the extra
Read/Write/Edit tools when you want diff cards and structured edits:

```sh
zua -workspace ./my-project                # pristine (default)
zua -workspace ./my-project -file-tools    # + Read/Write/Edit
```

The status line shows last-turn and cumulative session token usage, so you can
A/B both modes on your own workload.

## Install as a command

```sh
make install        # go install ./cmd/... → zua + zua-agent in ~/go/bin
```

Then run it inside any project directory (workspace = current directory):

```sh
cd ~/my-project
zua                                   # pristine config, workspace = .
zua -file-tools                       # with Read/Write/Edit + diff cards
zua -provider commandcode             # GLM-5.3-Flash via Command Code
```

`zua-agent` is the headless variant (JSON request in, JSONL events out).
# unreal-agent-tui design

Decisions locked with the project owner; implement in this order.

## Principles

- Wrap the public unreal-agent harness; never fork it. If a feature needs
  harness internals, defer until upstream supports it.
- Mirror pi's UX where it is cheap to do so; diverge only where the harness
  differs.

## Decisions

| Area | Decision |
| --- | --- |
| Tool safety | Auto-run all tools (pi default: no per-call approval). Revisit later; if added, gate at the operation-manager wrapper. |
| Rendering | Assistant text rendered as markdown (glamour) with syntax highlighting; tool calls as collapsible cards; Edit/Write cards show colorized diffs. |
| Streaming | Tool calls and statuses render as they arrive. **Token streaming deferred**: upstream's `IncludePartialMessages` is accepted but ignored — the adapter only returns complete responses and its SSE parsing is internal. Re-evaluate when the harness emits partials. |
| Sessions | Slash commands: `/new`, `/resume`, `/model [id]`, `/quit`, `/help`. Session picker lists `<workspace>/.harness/sessions/*.session.jsonl` by mtime with first user input as title. |
| Provider | Selected at startup via flag/env; `/model` switches model id for subsequent turns. |

## UI layout (alt-screen)

```
┌ header ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ unreal-agent · workspace · model · session 1a2b3c4 │
├ transcript (viewport, scrolls, auto-follow) ───────┤
│ ❯ user prompt (bold)                               │
│ · reasoning summary (dim italic)                   │
│ ⚙ Bash (bash)                                      │
│ ┌ diff card: Edit main.go ─────────────────────┐   │
│ │ - old line        + new line                 │   │
│ └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│ assistant markdown (glamour)                       │
├ status ────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ working… · last turn: 1.2k in / 0.3k out           │
├ editor (grows 1–8 lines with content) ─────────────┤
│ ❯ _                                                │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Keys: `Enter` send · `Esc` abort turn / quit when idle · `Ctrl+C` quit ·
`/`-commands in the editor.

## Streaming contract (runner → TUI JSONL)

First line: `{"type":"meta","session_id",...,"model","workspace"}` then
session-store items (`Kind`: input/turn/model_response/tool_call_status/fork)
and `{"type":"error"}`. The TUI decodes `model_response` output items
(message/tool_call/reasoning) and keeps a call_id → (name, arguments) map to
render tool cards when the matching `tool_call_status` arrives.

## Tool cards

- Decode arguments from the recorded `tool_call` item at card time (no I/O).
- `Edit`: colored `- old_text` / `+ new_text` lines (collapse to ~12 lines).
- `Write`: "create/replace path" + first lines of content, collapsed.
- `Read`: path (+offset/limit) only.
- `Bash`: command string truncated to one line.
- Non-terminal statuses render as pending; terminal update replaces the card
  line (matching by call_id in the transcript buffer).

## Session picker

Scan session files (mtime desc), title = first external input payload
(decoded JSON string, collapsed to 60 runes). `↑/↓` select, `Enter` load,
`Esc` cancel. Loading a session sets `session_id` and replays user inputs +
assistant messages from the file into the transcript (tool cards skipped).

## Out of scope (for now)

- Approval prompts (see Decisions), extensions/skills, themes, mouse support,
  image tools in the UI.

## Cost alignment (added after reviewing unreallabs.ai/blog/unreal-agent)

The published cost savings come from (a) minimal harness footprint — few tool
schemas, simple prompts, no sub-agents — and (b) more tool work per turn via
the async tool model. Their benchmark tables correlate more tool definitions
with more tool calls and input tokens (Pi: 27–60 tools → 57–75 calls;
unreal-agent: ~5 tools → 27–38).

Consequences for this project:

- **Pristine by default.** The runner now mirrors upstream exactly: Bash +
  ViewImage (+ SkillUse when skills exist), upstream default system prompt,
  $SHELL resolution, operation directory under the session store. No file
  tools, no extra prompt. This is the configuration their cost numbers were
  measured against.
- **File tools are opt-in** via `-file-tools` (runner flag or TUI flag, or
  `"file_tools": true` in the JSON request). They add schema tokens but may
  save turns on edit-heavy work; treat as an empirical, per-workload choice.
- **Usage in the status line**: the TUI accumulates per-turn and session
  input/output tokens from model_response usage, enabling direct A/B cost
  comparison between pristine and file-tools runs.

Here's my analysis of the project:

# unreal-agent-tui — Project Analysis

## What it is
A Go terminal UI ("pair-programming CLI") built on top of the [unreal-agent](https://github.com/unreallabsai/unreal-agent) harness (v0.1.1). It ships **two binaries**:

- **`zua`** — bubbletea TUI: transcript view, markdown rendering (glamour), tool-call cards with colorized diffs, session picker, usage/status line.
- **`zua-agent`** — headless runner: JSON request in → session events as JSONL out, resumable sessions stored under `<workspace>/.harness/sessions`.

## Architecture (~2,400 LOC, clean layering)

```
cmd/zua          → internal/tui        (UI: model, events, render, agent spawn, session picker)
cmd/zua-agent    → internal/runner     (wires harness: coordinator, inbox, contextbuilder, session store, LLM clients)
                 → internal/filetools  (Read/Write/Edit tools as translator + operation.Manager wrapper)
                 → internal/testsrv    (fake OpenAI Responses API for tests)
```

**Key design decisions (documented in DESIGN.md and consistently implemented):**
1. **Wrap, don't fork** the upstream harness — the runner composes public packages only.
2. **"Pristine by default"** — Bash + ViewImage only (matching upstream's cost benchmark), with Read/Write/Edit opt-in via `-file-tools`. A thoughtful cost-consciousness runs through the docs (tool-count vs. token-spend rationale).
3. **Durability via the operation-manager pattern** — file ops go through the same `operation.Manager` pipeline as Bash, so they're cancelable, recorded in session state, and resumable.
4. **Process-per-turn**: the TUI spawns `zua-agent` per prompt, streams JSONL over a pipe, abort via `context` cancellation. Simple and robust.

## Health check
- ✅ `go build ./cmd/...` passes; `go vet` clean; `bin/zua` + `bin/zua-agent` present
- ✅ `go test ./...` — all 3 test packages pass (`runner`, `filetools`, `tui`)
- ✅ Tests are real, not token: **end-to-end tests** run the actual agent against a fake SSE OpenAI server (testsrv) and assert files get written and sessions replay correctly; plus unit tests for path-escape rejection and R/W/E semantics

## Code quality observations

**Strengths**
- Excellent documentation discipline: README, DESIGN.md with locked decisions, and per-package doc comments explaining *why*.
- Dependency injection done right: `runner.Run(ctx, args, getenv, stdout, stderr)` makes it fully testable.
- Careful concurrency: `filetools.Manager` pump goroutine, mutex-guarded cancel map; TUI re-arms its single `listen()` with an explicit invariant comment.
- Good security hygiene: file tools reject workspace-escape paths (`../` traversal) — and it's tested.
- Nice touches: custom `itoa`/`trimFloat` to avoid fmt overhead in hot render path, glamour render caching keyed by width.

**Potential issues / improvement ideas**
1. **Silent error swallowing in the TUI stream** — `cmd.Stderr = io.Discard` in `agent.go` discards agent stderr; startup failures (missing API key, bad provider) may surface only as an opaque exit code. Surfacing stderr would notably improve UX.
2. **JSON field naming relies on Go defaults** (`Kind`, `CallID`, `InputTokens`… in `events.go`) — coupling the TUI to the harness's Go field capitalization; explicit tags would be more resilient to upstream renames.
3. **`m.events = make(chan tea.Msg, 256)`** — a slow UI could block the reader goroutine (events are sent unconditionally); 256 is a reasonable buffer but a drop-oldest policy or larger buffer might be safer on long turns.
4. **Edit tool writes files with `0o644` unconditionally** — loses the original file mode on Edit/Write over existing files.
5. **No token streaming** — acknowledged as deferred in DESIGN.md (upstream limitation), correctly out of scope.
6. Minor: `sort` in `events.go`/dead `sync` import comment in `model.go` suggest small cleanups; no CI config, no LICENSE file in the repo root.

## Verdict
A well-scoped, well-tested integration project with unusually good design documentation for its size. The layering is textbook (adapter/wrapper pattern around the harness, everything testable via injected fakes), and the "pristine vs. file-tools" cost framing shows real engagement with the upstream project's philosophy. The main low-hanging fruit is stderr visibility and wire-format hardening.

Data.Text:
Now that I've seen the full rendering layer, here's my honest take on the TUI:

## What I genuinely like

**The interaction model is right.** Spawn `zua-agent` per turn as a subprocess and stream JSONL back is exactly how pi/claude-code-style CLIs should work — a crash or hang in the agent can't take down the UI, abort is just `context` cancellation, and resumability falls out of the session store for free. It's the least-clever architecture that fully solves the problem, which is a compliment.

**The transcript design shows taste.** Tool cards matched by `call_id` (tool call appears the moment the model emits it, then the terminal status replaces it in place) is the correct UX — you see *what the agent is doing* while it does it, not a wall of text afterward. The Edit diff cards with `-`/`+` coloring and a `… N more changed lines` collapse are the single most valuable feature for trusting an agent in your repo, and they're rendered with zero I/O (decoded from recorded args, per DESIGN.md — nice discipline).

**Small pragmatic touches reveal experience:** glamour rendering cached per block *and* per width (re-render on resize only), the custom `itoa`/`trimFloat` in the usage line, editor growing 1→8 lines with Alt/Shift+Enter for newlines, `Esc` doubling as abort-when-running/quit-when-idle.

## Where I'd push back

1. **No scrolling affordance.** `refresh()` calls `GotoBottom()` unconditionally, so if you scroll up to read something while a turn is running, the next event yanks you back to the bottom. Auto-follow should disengage when the user scrolls up and re-engage when they return to the bottom. This is the most annoying real-world flaw.

2. **Stderr is thrown away** (`cmd.Stderr = io.Discard`). When the agent binary fails to start — missing API key, stale `zua-agent` next to an updated `zua` — you get `agent exited: exit status 1` and nothing else. For a tool whose first-run failure mode is "your env var isn't set," that's a bad first impression. Piping stderr into an error block would fix it cheaply.

3. **Diff cards for Edit are slightly misleading.** `renderDiff` prints *all* old lines then *all* new lines — not a real line-level diff. Fine for small edits, but replacing a 20-line block renders 40 lines (truncated to 16) where a real diff would show a 2-line hunk. A proper LCS-based hunk would be ~30 lines of code and materially better.

4. **The render path rebuilds the whole transcript on every event.** `refresh()` re-renders all blocks (`renderTranscript`) into one giant string on each tool status. Glamour blocks are cached, but lipgloss styles/wraps still re-run, and the string grows unboundedly over a long session. A long session (hundreds of blocks) will start to feel sluggish on resize. A dirty-block or ring-buffer approach would future-proof it.

5. **Tool cards only appear from `model_response` items** — meaning between the model finishing its response and the tool actually starting, and for the pristine config the card shows only `⚙ Bash $ cmd` with no live output. You can't see what a long-running command is printing until the turn ends. Even a one-line "last output" trickle would help. (Partly upstream's fault — no partial events — but the JSONL contract could carry completed tool output.)

6. **Minor nits:** the `parsing` of args handles the double-encoded JSON string quirk with a comment (good) but `parseArgs` silently swallows unmarshal errors; `turnUsage`/`sessionIn` accumulate even for aborted turns; and there's no visual distinction for the session picker when it's empty vs. loading beyond the spinner.

## Verdict

**7.5/10 as a working tool; the fundamentals are better than most hobby TUIs and the design doc shows it's built deliberately.** It already does the 20% that matters — you can see and trust what the agent did. The gaps are all polish-tier: scroll-follow behavior, stderr visibility, real diffs, and render performance on long sessions. None of them require architectural change; all four are a weekend of work.

Want me to fix any of these? The scroll-follow + stderr relay pair would be my first pick — highest UX payoff per line changed.

## Streaming contract (runner → TUI JSONL)

First line: `{"type":"meta","session_id",...,"model","workspace"}` then
session-store items (`Kind`: input/turn/model_response/tool_call_status/fork)
and `{"type":"error"}`. The TUI decodes `model_response` output items

render tool cards when the matching `tool_call_status` arrives.

- `Edit`: colored `- old_text` / `+ new_text` lines (collapse to ~12 lines).
- `Write`: "create/replace path" + first lines of content, collapsed.
- `Read`: path (+offset/limit) only.
- `Bash`: command string truncated to one line.

Scan session files (mtime desc), title = first external input payload

The published cost savings come from (a) minimal harness footprint — few tool
schemas, simple prompts, no sub-agents — and (b) more tool work per turn via
the async tool model. Their benchmark tables correlate more tool definitions
with more tool calls and input tokens (Pi: 27–60 tools → 57–75 calls;
unreal-agent: ~5 tools → 27–38).

  ViewImage (+ SkillUse when skills exist), upstream default system prompt,
  $SHELL resolution, operation directory under the session store. No file
  tools, no extra prompt. This is the configuration their cost numbers were
  measured against.

  `"file_tools": true` in the JSON request). They add schema tokens but may
  save turns on edit-heavy work; treat as an empirical, per-workload choice.
- **Usage in the status line**: the TUI accumulates per-turn and session
  input/output tokens from model_response usage, enabling direct A/B cost
  comparison between pristine and file-tools runs.

# CONTEXT.md Format

## Structure

```md
# {Context Name}

{One or two sentence description of what this context is and why it exists.}

## Language

**Order**:
{A one or two sentence description of the term}
_Avoid_: Purchase, transaction

**Invoice**:
A request for payment sent to a customer after delivery.
_Avoid_: Bill, payment request

**Customer**:
A person or organization that places orders.
_Avoid_: Client, buyer, account
```

## Rules

- **Be opinionated.** When multiple words exist for the same concept, pick the best one and list the others under `_Avoid_`.
- **Keep definitions tight.** One or two sentences max. Define what it IS, not what it does.
- **Only include terms specific to this project's context.** General programming concepts (timeouts, error types, utility patterns) don't belong even if the project uses them extensively. ```

- If only a root `CONTEXT.md` exists, single context

## Round 2

❓ **Q6 - Prompt box visual form**: Your stated priority. Options:
- (a) Rounded-corner bordered box (CC style): `╭─╮ │ ╰─╯` in dim border, `> ` inside, border brightens on focus
- (b) Keep borderless `❯ ` prompt, just restyle colors/spacing
- (c) Bordered box + a dim hint line underneath (`? shortcuts · shift+enter newline`)

➡️ **Recommended: (c).** The border is what makes it feel like CC; the hint line is nearly free and teaches the keys your redesign introduces.

❓ **Q7 - Slash-command autocomplete**: CC types `/` and gets a popup menu. That was option (c) in Q1 and you chose (b) — but with a bordered prompt box, a minimal variant (filter-as-you-type list above the box, ↑/↓+tab to complete, descriptions from the command table we already have) is maybe 100 lines. Include now, or firmly out of scope?

➡️ **Recommended: out of scope, but design the box so it *can* host a popup later** (i.e., don't hardcode box height).

❓ **Q8 - Editing keys**: Keep `Enter` send / `Alt|Shift+Enter` newline, or adopt CC's backslash-continuation too?

➡️ **Recommended: keep as-is.** It works, it's documented, and alt/shift+enter is the better UX anyway.

❓ **Q9 - Collapse defaults — the `⏺` one-liners**: When idle, what collapses to a single line? My proposed mapping:
- Tool cards → `⏺ Bash($ go test ./...) ⎿ ok` (Read: path+lines, Write: path+bytes, Edit: path +`+3/-1`)
- Reasoning → one dim line (already is)
- Assistant messages & user prompts → never collapse

➡️ **Recommended: that mapping.** The summary line for Edit needs an added/removed line count — computed at render time from the args we already decode, no I/O.

❓ **Q10 - The expand toggle**: Ctrl+O toggles "verbose transcript mode": all tool cards render fully expanded (current behavior), toggle again collapses to `⏺` lines. In-place re-render (blocks carry both renderings), not an overlay. Also: a fresh tool card while collapsed shows as its one-liner only.

➡️ **Recommended: exactly that.** Simple state flag + dual rendering, reuses the per-block cache with a `verbose` key.

❓ **Q11 - Spinner personality**: CC randomizes gerund verbs ("Reticulating pixels…"). Adopt (a small verb list, dim, next to the spinner), or keep `working…`?

➡️ **Recommended: adopt.** ~10 lines of code, disproportionately large charm payoff.

❓ **Q12 - Palette**: (a) Keep glamour's auto-style for markdown, restyle chrome (headers, cards, status) to dim gray + one accent color. (b) Also restyle markdown rendering to a custom muted theme. And what accent — cyan/12 (current title color), or something warmer?

➡️ **Recommended: (a) with accent = 12 (cyan) kept.** Custom glamour themes are a rabbit hole; chrome restyle is where 90% of the perceived polish is. Respect `NO_COLOR`.

❓ **Q13 - Status line contents**: Currently `working…`/`idle · tokens`. Add **mode** (`pristine`/`file-tools`) and current **model** there? Model is already in the header, but CC keeps it visible at the bottom near where you type.

➡️ **Recommended: yes — mode + model in the status line.** Mode especially: it's invisible today and it's the cost-critical setting.

❓ **Q14 - Mouse**: Keep mouse cell-motion enabled (current), or go keyboard-first and drop it (CC is keyboard-only; mouse capture can annoy terminal copy-paste)?

➡️ **Recommended: keep.** With alt-screen + collapsed entries, mouse scrolling is genuinely useful. Easy to drop later if it fights copy-paste.
